A la peine dans les sondages, Edouard Philippe présente un projet de droite classique et d’inspiration libérale, qu’il « assume massivement ». Des « réformes radicales », entre division par deux du nombre de titres de séjour, recours à la reconnaissance faciale ciblée et encadrée, indemnisation chômage limitée à 12 mois et règle d’or budgétaire pour ramener le déficit sous les 3 %. De quoi, espère le candidat Horizons, rassembler la droite et le centre, sans passer par la case primaire.
« Nada, aucun signe » : face au risque de censure sur le budget, les socialistes dénoncent l’absence de dialogue avec Sébastien Lecornu
« C’est un silence qui nous interroge ». Dans les rangs des parlementaires socialistes, on s’étonne du mutisme de Sébastien Lecornu sur le dénouement à venir de la séquence budgétaire – 49-3 ou ordonnances ? – et le risque non négligeable d’une censure pour l’exécutif d’ici quelques semaines. Alors que la première partie du projet de loi de finances pour 2027 a été rejetée en première lecture par l’Assemblée nationale le 4 novembre, le Sénat examinera le texte en séance publique à partir de vendredi. Or, à ce stade, aucune négociation n’a été entamée par le gouvernement avec les parlementaires des oppositions. À titre de comparaison : il y a tout juste un an, le Premier ministre multipliait les tractations avec le PS, pour un accord de non-censure et ainsi parvenir à maintenir un semblant de stabilité jusqu’en 2027, dans un contexte de forte fracturation politique.
« Là, nada, aucun signe », résume Patrick Kanner, le président du groupe PS, premier groupe d’opposition au Sénat. « J’ai vécu les négociations avec Michel Barnier, celles avec François Bayrou et celles avec Sébastien Lecornu, pour aboutir en 2025 à un budget de la Sécurité sociale voté, puisqu’il comprenait la suspension de la réforme des retraites, et à un projet de loi de finances adopté par 49-3 mais sans censure », rappelle l’élu du Nord. « À ce stade, nous n’avons même pas reçu un seul coup de téléphone. Je m’en suis inquiété auprès de plusieurs ministres. Nous restons à disposition du gouvernement s’il a envie d’engager un bout de débat », lâche-t-il.
Un budget qui « donne des gages à l’extrême droite »
« Pour parvenir à un compromis, il nous faudrait des bases. À ce jour, elles n’y sont pas. Il n’y a aucun signaux forts dans ce texte, sur la justice fiscale par exemple », soupire Thierry Cozic, le président socialiste de la Commission des finances du Sénat. Même constat pour le budget de la Sécurité sociale : la majorité sénatoriale de droite et du centre a obtenu cette semaine le rétablissement de la réforme des retraites de 2023, et le report de la baisse des allègements de cotisations patronales. La gauche reproche au gouvernement son opposition timorée sur ces deux mesures. « À ce stade des discussions, nous avons un projet de budget qui est très marqué à droite, je dirais même qu’il donne des gages à l’extrême droite, sur l’Aide médicale d’Etat (AME) par exemple. Il y a peut-être une volonté d’aller chercher une non-censure du côté de l’extrême droite », avance Thierry Cozic.
« Le gouvernement choisit ses partenaires, s’il veut se tourner vers le Rassemblement national, il devrait avoir en mémoire la jurisprudence Barnier », avertit Patrick Kanner. Pour mémoire : le 4 décembre 2024, le gouvernement de Michel Barnier a été renversé au bout de trois mois grâce aux voix des députés d’extrême droite, qui avaient fait preuve jusque-là d’une certaine mansuétude à l’égard du Premier ministre, dénonçant notamment son projet de désindexation des petites retraites.
Sébastien Lecornu va lister « les thèmes prioritaires de discussion »
Ce mercredi, lors de la séance de questions au gouvernement, le gouvernement s’est défendu de chercher à envoyer des signaux à l’extrême droite. « Nous souhaitons pouvoir forger un compromis avec la droite républicaine et la gauche républicaine pour donner au pays un budget qui est plus que nécessaire », a assuré David Amiel, le ministre de l’Action et des Comptes publics. « Le Premier ministre aura l’occasion dans les prochains jours de lister les thèmes prioritaires de discussion », a-t-il précisé. Avec une ligne rouge : ramener le déficit sous la barre des 5 %.
En attendant, la gauche fourbit ses armes et compte profiter des débats au Sénat pour fixer ses propres priorités. À lui seul, le groupe PS a prévu de porter quelque 200 amendements sur la première partie du texte, c’est-à-dire celle consacrée aux recettes. Avec dans son viseur de nombreuses niches fiscales, mais aussi la sempiternelle question de la taxation des hauts revenus. « Ce budget est déjà obsolète, puisqu’il s’appuie sur une estimation de croissance à 1 %, alors que l’on sait déjà qu’elle sera plutôt à 0,3 ou 0,4 %. Nous sommes à la limite de l’insincérité », tempête Thierry Cozic. « Nous ne contestons pas la nécessité de redresser les comptes publics, mais nous disons qu’un autre budget est possible, et même nécessaire », explique la sénatrice PS Florence Blatrix-Contat, l’une des principales oratrices de son groupe sur ce texte.
« Il n’y a que des candidats dans l’hémicycle »
Toutefois, les éventuelles négociations pourraient tourner court face à un calendrier électoral qui risque de compliquer l’équation, en poussant les uns et les autres aux postures partisanes plutôt qu’à la recherche constructive de compromis. « On est déjà en campagne, il n’y a que des candidats dans l’hémicycle. C’est très compliqué », analysait fin octobre un cadre PS à l’Assemblée. Et d’ajouter : « S’il y a une motion de censure, cette fois je ne vois pas comment les socialistes ne la voteraient pas en majorité. »

SOURCE 1 (Le Monde) :
« C’est une honte absolue (…) Le seul reliquat de l’ambition écologique du macronisme vient de se faire rayer d’un trait de plume par l’extrême droite. » La députée écologiste Julie Laernoes (Loire-Atlantique) ne décolère pas : dans la soirée du mardi 17 novembre, dans le cadre de l’examen du projet de loi « relance du logement », l’Assemblée nationale a voté un amendement du Rassemblement national supprimant l’interdiction progressive de louer les passoires thermiques. Les députés sont ainsi revenus, par 108 voix pour contre 102, sur une disposition phare de la loi Climat et résilience de 2021 : l’obligation, pour louer, de rénover un logement dont le diagnostic de performance énergétique (DPE) est classé G, et de le faire d’ici 2028 pour les biens classés F puis d’ici 2034 pour la catégorie E.
Un amendement qui va bien plus loin que les assouplissements contenus dans le projet de loi du gouvernement. « C’est très très grave de céder ainsi au populisme climatique, selon lequel les règles sont la cause de la pénurie de logements, alors que les canicules vont se multiplier. Ce sont les personnes plus précaires qui vivent dans ces passoires thermiques », dénonce la députée Shéhérazade Bentorki (Nord, La France insoumise, LFI). Sa collègue Valérie Létard (Nord, Libertés, indépendants, outre-mer et territoires), qui a précédé Vincent Jeanbrun au ministère du logement, considère que « ce vote marque un tournant dans l’examen du texte, et risque de fragiliser et d’abîmer durablement la politique du logement ».

Passoires thermiques : l’Assemblée nationale vote la suppression des interdictions de location liées au DPE
L’interdiction de louer des passoires thermiques pourrait bientôt appartenir au passé. Les députés ont adopté, mardi 17 novembre dans la soirée, un amendement du Rassemblement national visant à supprimer les restrictions de location fondées sur le diagnostic de performance énergétique (DPE). Un vote serré, acquis à 108 voix contre 102, qui va bien au-delà du simple assouplissement défendu par le gouvernement dans son projet de loi sur le logement.
Déposé par Frédéric Falcon (Rassemblement national), l’amendement n° 85 supprime les principales dispositions de l’article 160 de la loi Climat et Résilience. Le projet de loi initial prévoyait pourtant une évolution moins radicale : il devait permettre, sous certaines conditions, de continuer à louer des logements classés F ou G, notamment lorsque leurs propriétaires s’engagent à réaliser des travaux ou que des contraintes techniques ou juridiques en empêchent la réalisation. L’adoption de l’amendement RN remet en cause l’ensemble de ce calendrier d’interdiction.
Pour justifier sa proposition, Frédéric Falcon dénonce « un système devenu excessivement complexe et source d’insécurité juridique ». « Confrontés au coût des travaux, à l’instabilité des règles et à la perspective d’une interdiction de louer, de nombreux propriétaires arbitrent en faveur de la vente, avec le risque de multiplier les congés pour vente et d’aggraver encore la pénurie locative », explique le député dans les motifs de son amendement. Il estime que la rénovation énergétique « doit être encouragée par l’incitation, l’accompagnement et l’innovation plutôt que par l’interdiction de louer ».
Lors des débats, Vincent Jeanbrun (LR) avait défendu une approche différente, reconnaissant la volonté de certains parlementaires de « redonner de la liberté » aux propriétaires, mais insistant sur la nécessité de maintenir « un plan ambitieux de rénovation » du bâti. Il a notamment invoqué les enjeux de pouvoir d’achat, d’environnement et de souveraineté énergétique.
« Le gouvernement propose, le Parlement dispose » a réagit l’entourage du ministre après le vote, tout en disant que cette décision ne correspond « évidemment ni à la position du gouvernement ni à celle du ministre ».
Quatre députés signalent une erreur de vote
L’issue du scrutin aurait pu être différente. Trois députés comptabilisés parmi les voix favorables à l’amendement — Melouka Hadj-Mimoune (groupe socialiste), Sandrine Lalanne et Jean-François Rousset (Ensemble pour la République) — ont indiqué avoir voulu voter contre. Lionel Duparay (Droite républicaine) a, pour sa part, déclaré avoir souhaité s’abstenir.
En tenant compte de ces quatre rectifications, l’amendement aurait été rejeté par 105 voix contre 104. Le règlement de l’Assemblée nationale ne permettant pas de modifier un vote après la clôture du scrutin, son adoption demeure pour l'instant acquise.
La configuration du vote témoigne d'une mobilisation plus importante des groupes de droite et d’extrême droite. Les 76 députés du Rassemblement national présents ont été rejoints par 15 élus de la Droite républicaine et sept de l’Union des droites pour la République. Du côté d’Ensemble pour la République, seuls 26 des 90 députés ont voté contre l’amendement.
Les associations vent debout
L’adoption de l’amendement a suscité des réactions critiques parmi les acteurs de la rénovation énergétique et de la défense des locataires. Manuel Domergue, directeur des études de la Fondation pour le logement, a dénoncé auprès de l’AFP « la victoire d'un populisme climatique », qu'il considère comme « une catastrophe pour les locataires ». Il a demandé au gouvernement d’obtenir un nouveau vote.
Damien Barbosa, porte-parole du réseau Cler et coordinateur du collectif Rénovons, a également critiqué le vote : «C’est la lutte des classes qui s’est jouée ici, et ce vote est un vote de classe. Une passoire en location sur deux appartient aux 30 % des ménages les plus riches. Au nom d’une crise du logement née de la surcaptation du logement en location par les 3,5 % des plus riches et de la spéculation, les députés ont choisi leur camp : faire un cadeau aux plus riches, et laisser les classes populaires se ruiner en hiver, et risquer leur vie en été ».
Les députés écologistes et de La France insoumise avaient, de leur côté, tenté sans succès de supprimer l’assouplissement prévu dans le projet de loi. La députée LFI Anaïs Belouassa-Cherifi a notamment rappelé que le « logement est une question de santé publique », accusant le gouvernement « d'exonérer les bailleurs » pour faire « payer la facture aux locataires ».
Une seconde délibération encore possible
Manuel Domergue a appelé le gouvernement à provoquer une nouvelle délibération. Prévue par l’article 101 du règlement de l’Assemblée nationale, cette procédure peut être demandée par le gouvernement ou un député avant le début des explications de vote sur l’ensemble du texte. Elle permet de réexaminer tout ou partie du projet de loi. Si la demande émane du gouvernement ou de la commission parlementaire chargée d’examiner le texte, la seconde délibération est accordée de droit.
A ce stade, l’entourage de Vincent Jeanbrun n’a pas annoncé que l’exécutif comptait y recourir. Dans l’attente d’une éventuelle modification législative, les interdictions de location liées au DPE restent en vigueur. Le projet de loi doit encore poursuivre son parcours parlementaire, avec notamment une commission mixte paritaire chargée de trouver un accord entre députés et sénateurs.
ANRU 3, opérations d’intérêt local et reconstruction après sinistre
Plusieurs autres mesures ont également été adoptées au cours de l’examen du projet de loi. Les députés ont approuvé le lancement d’un troisième programme national de renouvellement urbain (ANRU 3), ainsi que la création d’opérations d’intérêt local (OIL). Ces périmètres permettront aux communes de déroger, sous certaines conditions, aux règles d’urbanisme pour accélérer la production de logements. En contrepartie, les biens concernés devront rester affectés à la résidence principale pendant quinze ans, sans pouvoir devenir des résidences secondaires ou des locations touristiques.
Un autre amendement du gouvernement a été adopté pour faciliter la reconstruction après des sinistres de grande ampleur. Il prévoit la possibilité d'activer par décret un dispositif dérogatoire destiné à accélérer la reconstruction des bâtiments détruits ou endommagés, notamment à la suite d'événements tels que les incendies de l'été 2026.
Le vote sur l’ensemble du projet de loi est prévu le mardi 24 novembre à l’Assemblée nationale.

SOURCE 1 (Public Sénat) :
A la peine dans les sondages, Edouard Philippe présente un projet de droite classique et d’inspiration libérale, qu’il « assume massivement ». Des « réformes radicales », entre division par deux du nombre de titres de séjour, recours à la reconnaissance faciale ciblée et encadrée, indemnisation chômage limitée à 12 mois et règle d’or budgétaire pour ramener le déficit sous les 3 %. De quoi, espère le candidat Horizons, rassembler la droite et le centre, sans passer par la case primaire.
Soldats français en Ukraine : la ministre déléguée auprès de la ministre des Armées auditionnée au Sénat, le 25 novembre prochain
« Je n’étais pas au courant ». Le président de la commission des affaires étrangères, de la défense et des forces armées du Sénat, Cédric Perrin (LR), a réagi au micro de Public Sénat aux révélations de RFI sur la présence de soldats français en Ukraine. D’après Radio France internationale, la force nommée « Volia » et dirigée par un général français s’appuie sur le détachement Gerfaut officiellement déployé en Pologne dans le cadre de la mission européenne EUMAM-Ukraine destinée à soutenir les actions de formation des soldats ukrainiens.
L’article 35 de la Constitution impose au gouvernement d’informer le Parlement de sa décision de faire intervenir les forces armées à l’étranger. Une information qui peut donner lieu à un débat qui n’est suivi d’aucun vote. « La question qui doit se poser ici, c’est: est-ce que c’était une opération extérieure ou non ? De mon point de vue, ce n’en était pas une », a expliqué Cédric Perrin, comparant avec des opérations de formation des forces armées sénégalaises, djiboutiennes ou centrafricaines, qui n’ont pas donné lieu au déclenchement de l’article 35.
« Le gouvernement a fait preuve de beaucoup d’amateurisme dans cette affaire »
Toutefois, d’un point de vue politique, pour le sénateur, cette information aurait « nécessité a minima une communication du gouvernement aux commissions concernées ou aux présidents des assemblées concernées ». « Ça me semblait la moindre des choses. Je pense que le gouvernement a fait preuve de beaucoup d’amateurisme dans cette affaire. Ça dénote aussi une certaine forme de mépris du Parlement », a-t-il déploré.
La ministre déléguée auprès de la ministre des Armées et des Anciens combattants, Alice Rufo, sera auditionnée mercredi prochain à 8 h 30 par la commission des affaires étrangères, de la défense et des forces armées du Sénat, a annoncé Cédric Perrin. L’audition se tiendra à huis clos. Les sénateurs chercheront à savoir « concrètement l’implication des forces françaises conventionnelles en Ukraine ».

SOURCE 2 (laclepublique.fr) :
« Je n’étais pas au courant. » C’est ainsi que Cédric Perrin, président de la commission des affaires étrangères et de la défense du Sénat, a réagi ce mercredi 18 novembre aux révélations sur la présence de militaires français en Ukraine.
Deux jours plus tôt, RFI révélait l’existence d’une mission confidentielle baptisée Volia. Depuis plusieurs mois, selon les informations de la presse, de petits détachements français se relaient sur le territoire ukrainien pour former des militaires et participer à l’entretien des équipements livrés par la France.
Le gouvernement reconnaît désormais cette présence. Alice Rufo, ministre déléguée aux Armées, a précisé mercredi sur RMC que ces personnels ne constituaient pas des unités combattantes et intervenaient loin du front. Elle sera auditionnée le 25 novembre à huis clos par les sénateurs.
L’affaire soulève une question qui dépasse largement le soutien à l’Ukraine : qui décide du moment à partir duquel un engagement militaire français mérite d’être soumis au contrôle du Parlement ?
Trois jours, quatre mois
Jusqu’en 2008, la Constitution ne prévoyait l’autorisation du Parlement que pour les déclarations de guerre. Or, sous la Ve République, la France n’a jamais formellement déclaré la guerre. Elle a pourtant engagé ses forces dans de nombreux conflits.
La révision constitutionnelle de 2008 a instauré deux échéances. Le gouvernement doit informer le Parlement dans les trois jours suivant le début d’une intervention militaire à l’étranger et solliciter son autorisation pour la poursuivre au-delà de quatre mois.
Depuis cette réforme, la procédure d’autorisation a été utilisée à sept reprises, notamment pour les interventions en Afghanistan, en Libye, au Mali et en Irak. La dernière remonte au 25 novembre 2015, pour l’engagement des forces aériennes françaises en Syrie.
Onze ans sans nouveau vote au titre de l’article 35.
En janvier 2026, la France a encore mené, conjointement avec le Royaume-Uni, des frappes contre l’État islamique en Syrie. Comme le relève un rapport de l’Assemblée nationale publié en février, l’autorisation accordée en 2015 restait valable : la Constitution n’impose aucun renouvellement périodique.
Le Parlement peut néanmoins se prononcer par d’autres moyens. En mars 2024, les élus avaient ainsi voté sur la politique française de soutien à l’Ukraine à l’occasion de la présentation de l’accord de sécurité entre les deux pays.
Une frontière que l’exécutif trace lui-même
Toute présence militaire à l’étranger ne constitue évidemment pas une intervention au sens de la Constitution. Des soldats français participent régulièrement à des exercices internationaux ou assurent des missions de formation.
Mais la distinction devient plus délicate lorsque ces activités se déroulent dans un pays en guerre.
Pour déterminer si l’article 35 s’applique, le gouvernement tient notamment compte de trois critères : l’importance des moyens engagés, les risques auxquels sont exposés les militaires et l’existence d’une intention de combattre.
Ces difficultés de qualification sont bien antérieures à l’affaire Volia.
En avril 2026, un rapport de la commission des finances du Sénat relevait que les missions françaises de réassurance sur le flanc oriental de l’OTAN n’étaient pas classées parmi les opérations extérieures (OPEX), notamment pour éviter d’envoyer le signal d’un affrontement direct avec la Russie.
Cette classification administrative, qui détermine certains droits supplémentaires des militaires en cas de blessure ou de décès, est distincte de l’application de l’article 35. Mais elle illustre combien la dénomination d’une mission peut aussi répondre à des considérations diplomatiques.
Le secret militaire n’impose pas le silence parlementaire
Le soutien apporté sur place aux Ukrainiens répond à une logique opérationnelle compréhensible. Réparer un équipement au sein du pays évite de devoir l’acheminer jusqu’en Pologne. Le 9 novembre, l’Union européenne a d’ailleurs décidé d’établir une présence en Ukraine pour mieux coordonner ses activités de formation militaire.
Reste la question du risque. Les personnels français évoluent sur le territoire d’un pays régulièrement frappé par des missiles et des drones russes.
Cédric Perrin estime lui-même que la mission ne relève pas nécessairement de l’article 35. Il considère néanmoins que les commissions compétentes auraient dû être informées.
Une telle communication confidentielle était possible dès le début de la mission, sans dévoiler les effectifs, les déplacements ou les lieux d’intervention au public. Elle ne nécessitait aucune réforme constitutionnelle ni autorisation préalable.
Alors que la France participe aux discussions sur les futures garanties de sécurité de l’Ukraine, la distinction mérite d’être clarifiée.
Le Parlement n’a pas vocation à diriger les opérations militaires. Il doit, en revanche, pouvoir comprendre quels risques la France accepte de prendre avant d’avoir à en assumer les conséquences.

SOURCE 1 (Al Jazeera) :
Pete Hegseth has unveiled a new military deal with Venezuela in his first visit since the US capture of Nicolas Maduro.

SOURCE 2 (CNN) :
The United States has signed a new agreement to reestablish military ties with Venezuela more than 10 months after toppling its leader in a military raid, US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced during his first trip to the South American nation on Wednesday.
“Venezuela has gone from our most aggressive regional threat to a compliant security partner,” Hegseth said outside the US Embassy in Caracas.
The Pentagon chief described the deal as “historic,” saying it would allow American and Venezuelan forces to train together and share intelligence, defense equipment and other capabilities.
He insisted that the partnership would not be “cosmetic” and would require defense and security reforms in Venezuela to modernize its military and eliminate “persistent threats” to both nations.
The timeline and scope of the deal remain unclear.
The Defense Department has not responded to questions about the agreement or Hegseth’s trip, nor did it provide a daily schedule for the secretary on the day of his visit.
Hegseth appeared to have signed the agreement earlier at the Venezuelan presidential palace with Defense Minister Gustavo Gonzalez Lopez, according to footage broadcast on state TV.
In a televised meeting with Venezuela’s acting President Delcy Rodriguez, Hegseth said the US looks forward to deepening their defense cooperation “to ensure the Venezuelan people are not threatened by foreign actors or narco-terrorists or criminals and that they are safe and secure inside sovereign borders.”
Rodriguez said their renewed “technical-military cooperation” is meant to confront common threats and make the region safer.
Both Hegseth and Rodriguez underscored their countries’ remarkable turn in relations since the US captured Venezuela’s authoritarian leader Nicolas Maduro on January 3.
“The weight of this moment does not escape me,” Hegseth said outside the embassy. “Just one year ago, my presence here, our presence here would have been deemed impossible.”
Rodriguez said, “We have turned very difficult and very harsh moments for our people … into an extraordinary space for cooperation and the mutual benefit of our countries.”
Since Maduro’s capture, the US has been working with the acting Venezuelan government on the country’s democratic transition and political reconciliation.
Rodriguez has met just about every demand from Washington, including releasing hundreds of political prisoners and making it easier for US companies to invest in the country.
Wednesday’s military deal is the latest effort by the Trump administration to bolster security cooperation with Latin American countries with the aim of combating what it calls “designated terrorist organizations” in the region.
Hegseth traveled to Colombia later on Wednesday and was expected to discuss security ties and deliver military equipment, according to the Colombian defense minister.
That visit comes amid a New York Times report that said Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella this week rejected a US plan for joint anti-crime operations on Colombian soil.
A source from Colombia’s Ministry of Defense told CNN that while the government supports increased military cooperation and the intelligence sharing to combat drug cartels and terrorist organizations, it cannot greenlight operations involving foreign forces on the ground, as this requires legislative authorization.
Hegseth is also expected to travel to Ecuador and Honduras as part of a tour of Latin America.
CNN’s Anabella Gonzalez, Mauricio Torres, Fernando Ramos and Haley Britzky contributed to this report.

SOURCE 1 (Politico) :
It's the first time in 18 years a Democrat has won a Senate race in the state.

SOURCE 2 (MS NOW) :
Democrat Mary Peltola has unseated Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, expanding Democrats’ new Senate majority to 56 seats in a midterm wave that also gave the party control of the House.
Peltola, a former congresswoman who is Yup’ik, will be the first Alaska Native to serve in the Senate. She is also the first Democrat to win a Senate race in Alaska since Mark Begich in 2008. Sullivan unseated Begich six years later.
The Associated Press called the race for Peltola after an update from Alaska’s Division of Elections put her above 50% of the vote. Her lead had grown significantly in the days before that update, and MS NOW had shifted its rating of the contest to “likely Democratic.” Alaska uses ranked choice voting, which lets voters rank up to four candidates. But if Peltola stays above 50% of first-choice votes in the final count, no ranked choice tabulation will be needed.
In a video statement posted after the race was called, Peltola thanked supporters for trusting her and ensured Alaskans that she would be “guided by your voices every step of the way.”
“It’s clear that the status quo in D.C. cannot go on any longer. Alaskans have voted for change and I am so honored to be your next U.S. senator,” Peltola said.
She added, “We need to fight corruption and corporate greed. We need to bring prices down, we need to lower fuel costs and build new homes. And we need to ensure Alaskans are served by your elected senators.”
The result is a sharp turn for a state that President Donald Trump carried by about 13 percentage points in 2024. Trump went to Alaska in October to rally for Sullivan, a Marine veteran and former state attorney general who was seeking a third term.
But Trump turned out to be a drag on Sullivan. Alaska voters showed a clear appetite for stronger checks on a president many of them felt had made things worse in their state. According to the MS NOW Voter Poll, Trump’s job rating in Alaska is underwater, and a majority of voters said Sullivan was too supportive of him. Two-thirds said the GOP-controlled Congress has not done enough to put checks and balances on the presidency.
The poll found that Peltola won more than 5% of Trump’s 2024 voters and decisively carried people who did not vote in 2024. Among her supporters, the quality that mattered most was bringing “needed change.”
Before Peltola entered the race in January, Republicans were heavily favored to hold the seat. But she was one of the few Democrats who could say she had already won statewide in Alaska. In a 2022 special election, she succeeded the late Rep. Don Young and became the first Alaska Native to Congress. She then lost re-election in 2024 to Republican Nick Begich by fewer than 3 points.

SOURCE 1 (Politico Europe) :
BRUSSELS — EU lawmakers from across the political spectrum say they have come under pressure from the Chinese government for traveling to or communicating with Taiwan.
Eight MEPs gave accounts of what some described as intimidation inside the European Parliament — including a senior Chinese diplomat turning up unannounced at one MEP’s office — detentions at the Chinese border and threatening letters.
The incidents come a little over a year after the European Parliament and Beijing restored ties following years of fraught relations over European criticism of China’s treatment of ethnic and religious minorities, and against the backdrop of European manufacturers creaking under the competitive pressure of Chinese imports.

SOURCE 2 (Mezha.net) :
EU lawmakers say China pressured them over Taiwan ties
Photo source: Politico
Several MEPs say Chinese officials sought to deter their travel to or communications with Taiwan. Parliament President Roberta Metsola is in contact with Chinese authorities over the reported incidents.
Eight EU lawmakers from across the political spectrum described pressure they say they faced from the Chinese government. Their accounts included a senior Chinese diplomat’s unannounced visit to an MEP’s office, a lawmaker being detained at the Chinese border and letters urging MEPs to avoid official contact with Taiwan.
This is reported by Politico.
The accounts come a little over a year after the European Parliament and Beijing restored ties following years of strained relations over European criticism of China’s treatment of ethnic and religious minorities. Taiwan has been politically separate from China since 1949. Beijing claims the island, home to 23 million people, as part of its territory; the EU and its member countries do not recognize Taiwan as a separate country.
Engin Eroglu, a German liberal MEP who chairs the Parliament’s delegation to China, said he had received “fierce” pushback from Beijing but did not specify what it involved. “I have never encountered such behavior from foreign diplomats,” he said. The Chinese mission to the EU did not reply to requests for comment.
Before a June 2025 visit to Taiwan, António Tânger Corrêa, vice-chair of the far-right Patriots group, said a senior Chinese diplomat came to his office unannounced and warned that they “could not ensure” his safety and “didn’t know what could happen” if he travelled. Corrêa said Metsola offered to warn the Chinese mission or take tougher action, but he urged her to pursue diplomacy first.
MEPs who attended a forum in Taipei in October 2026 received letters, seen by POLITICO, from China’s EU mission urging them to “refrain from any official exchange in whatever form with the Taiwan authorities.” Czech MEP Ondřej Krutílek, who received a letter, said: “China has no right to intimidate elected representatives or interfere with their parliamentary work.” Other recipients included Michal Kobosko, Rihard Kols, Bernard Guetta and Michael Gahler.
Kobosko called the letter “bizarre” and said, “We cannot accept acts of direct pressure against us.” Guetta said meetings with China were usually “completely polite,” but the letter was sent “to try pressure.” Kols described its tone as “quite aggressive,” while saying he did not see it as grounds to tighten access rules for Chinese officials or ask Metsola to intervene.
Markéta Gregorová, a Czech Green MEP and vice-chair of the Parliament’s China delegation, said Chinese officials stopped her at Beijing border control on Sept. 26, confiscated her passport and barred her from using her phone. She said she was surrounded by police and held for about an hour and a half. “It was an extremely unpleasant experience and, without my colleagues there to help me, it would have been frightening,” she told POLITICO.
Gregorová is leading the revision of the Cybersecurity Act, a proposal that could exclude Chinese telecom suppliers from European networks. Chinese officials have threatened “countermeasures” if it passes. Gregorová said she did not know whether the border incident was an administrative error or a “deliberate intimidation tactic.” She said she was sending a letter to China’s National People’s Congress demanding an explanation and would ask Metsola to bar Chinese representatives from Parliament unless one was provided.
Metsola has been in close contact with the MEPs concerned and “has conveyed our questions and concerns directly to the Chinese authorities,” her spokesperson, Juri Laas, said. “Diplomatic contacts are ongoing in an effort to ensure that further incidents can be avoided.” Laas added that MEPs should be able to exercise their freedom of mandate and that members travelling with an official Parliament delegation should not have problems entering their host country.
Earlier in 2026, POLITICO reported that Chinese officials had told MEPs in the Socialists and Democrats group not to vote for a report critical of Beijing, warning of possible consequences. In 2021, Beijing sanctioned five MEPs after EU sanctions targeting alleged abuses of Uyghur rights. The Parliament responded by freezing ratification of an EU-China investment deal and halting diplomatic contact with Beijing.
Other news you may find interesting:
- European Parliament lawmakers have proposed a NATO-linked defense union that could act independently in certain circumstances, with Ukraine, the UK and Norway identified as potential partners.
- Donald Trump rejected a report that Chinese entities provided Iran with satellite images of a Jordanian military base before an attack that killed three US troops.
- Trump-backed Republican Senate candidate Darline Graham said national security is not her area of expertise after struggling to answer a question about Taiwan and the South China Sea.

Investment and Governance: Through The Lens of Sustainability
Jitendra Aswani and Roberto Rigobon
NBER Working Paper No. 36011
November 2026
JEL No. G30
ABSTRACT
Using 3,944 sustainable bond issuances by public firms from 2013 to 2022, we examine the causal 
effect of sustainable investment on governance adoption. A heteroskedasticity-based identification 
strategy reveals that a 1% increase in sustainable debt (by total debt) raises the likelihood of 
sustainable governance adoption by 9.2%. Such adoption improves environmental performance by 
16% (structural estimates). These effects are confined to non-financial firms; for financial firms, 
governance adoption alone is in-sufficient, as sustainable loan borrowers environmental 
performance does not improve. Firms with stronger environmental performance are less likely to 
adopt sustainable governance. Results are robust to alternative definitions and extensive 
specification checks.
Jitendra Aswani
Massachusetts Institute of Technology
jaswani@corpgov.law.harvard.edu
Roberto Rigobon
Massachusetts Institute of Technology
MIT Sloan School of Management
and NBER
rigobon@mit.edu
ECGI Blog entry is available at 
https://www.ecgi.global/publications/blog/does-sustainable-investment-inspire-sustainable-
governance
1. INTRODUCTION
Achieving global climate objectives necessitates targeted financial commitments. According
to one estimate, a monumental investment exceeding $270 trillion is required for decar-
bonization efforts to realize the net-zero ambitions by 2050, which translates to an annual
investment of around $9.4 trillion.1 The global fixed income market stands as a pivotal pil-
lar for gathering the requisite capital for this climate transition. In 2022 alone, this market
reached an unprecedented total of $122 trillion, with the corporate debt sector contribut-
ing about 32%. Within this context, sustainable debt has experienced a significant surge,
reaching $3.7 trillion, with corporate sustainable debt comprising approximately half of this
amount, or about $1.7 trillion.2
Given the pivotal role of corporate sustainable debt in facilitating the transition to a
more climate-resilient economy, existing research predominantly focuses on clarifying the
phenomenon of greenium (Flammer [2021]; P´astor et al. [2022]; Aswani and Rajgopal [2025])
or on delving into the investment preferences of stakeholders within this sector (refer to Baker

tices plays a critical role in determining whether investments are channelled solely towards
financial gains or whether they also address and reduce a firm’s adverse environmental im-
pacts. In this paper, we explore this under-researched area by investigating whether sus-
tainable investment motivates firms to make changes in their organizational structure, such
as adopting sustainable governance. Drawing on the extensive literature on signaling in
economics, finance, and related disciplines3, we hypothesize that firms that care about sus-
tainable investment would undertake necessary changes in their organizational structure to
signal their commitment to the market, even if such signals are costly. Firms would adopt
these governance changes because sustainable debt issuance requires reporting compliance,
which includes the development of impact reports, use-of-proceeds accounts, and third-party
certifications required under green bond principles. These changes in governance would help
achieve compliance levels and attain the targeted environmental performance. Therefore,
these governance changes would be an observable signal for investors that firms are serious
about implementing sustainable projects.
As the literature on the governance impact of investment shows, firms alter corporate

issue, it is difficult to determine whether the firm is signaling to existing investors or at-
tempting to attract new investments. We address this simultaneity issue using identification
through heteroskedasticity and demonstrate that sustainable investment leads to changes
in sustainable governance. Furthermore, we provide causal evidence on whether a firm’s
adoption of sustainable governance effectively streamlines sustainable investment and, more
importantly, mitigates negative externalities, or if it merely serves as an advertising gimmick

Corporations engage in sustainable debt financing through two principal methods: they
either commit to dedicating the funds solely to environmentally friendly projects or opt to
tie the cost of borrowing to future environmental risks. The market segment characterized
by restrictions on the use of proceeds typically features participation from large, financially
robust firms with superior credit ratings (Aswani and Rajgopal [2025]). Green bonds, social
bonds, and sustainability bonds fall under this category. In contrast, sustainable debt in-
struments (such as sustainability-linked bonds) that integrate environmental risk into bond
features see more diverse participation across various industry sectors. Issuers of these bonds
adhere to restrictions on the use of funds, which are limited to specific categories, includ-
ing Energy, Energy Efficiency, Green Buildings and Infrastructure, Agriculture, Forestry,
Climate Change Adaptation and Mitigation, Waste Management, Clean Water, Pollution
Control, and Circular Economy, as outlined in the Green Bond Principles. To monitor the
development of these green projects, firms need to implement changes in governance for the
management of proceeds and to evaluate the impact of these projects.
To empirically examine whether sustainable investment motivates firms to adopt sus-
tainable governance, we gather sustainable fixed income data from the Bloomberg Global
Fixed Income and Environmental Finance databases, with sustainability governance metrics
extracted from BoardEx. Additionally, we collect data on firm fundamentals from World-
scope and Global Compustat. Upon merging these databases, the final dataset comprises
6,925 firms from 2013 to 2022, yielding 59,019 firm-year observations. Of these, 30% (3,053
firms) have implemented significant organizational changes to promote sustainability during
the observed period. Our sample also includes sustainable debt issuers that issued 3,944 sus-
tainable bonds between 2013 and 2022. Of these issuances, 3,056 are green bonds, with the
remainder comprising other sustainable debt instruments. The sample firms are primarily
from the financial, industrial, healthcare, materials, and consumer discretionary sectors. Ge-
ographically, a significant portion of these sustainable firms are located in the United States,
2
the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Canada, and Australia. This geographical distribu-
tion closely mirrors the distribution of issuers of sustainable debt, which is predominantly
from the United States, France, Germany, the United Kingdom, and China, suggesting a
correlation between organizational sustainability changes and sustainable debt issuance.
To evaluate sustainable debt at the firm-year level, we consider two indicators: the ratio
of cumulative sustainable debt issued (scaled by total debt) and the natural logarithm of the
total number of sustainable bonds issued. We define sustainable governance using a binary
variable that equals 1 for firms that appoint a chief sustainability officer (CSO) or establish
a sustainability committee, and 0 otherwise. To enhance the validity of our governance
metrics, we supplement our analysis with data from the Refinitiv ESG database. To test
our hypothesis, we conduct panel regressions with country, year, and industry fixed effects.
We find that a 1% increase in the amount of sustainable debt (as a proportion of total debt
issued) improves sustainable governance by 9.2%. These results suggest that sustainable
debt issuances inspire firms to introduce organizational changes for sustainability, paving
the way for sustainable governance. We are aware of endogeneity concerns, particularly
reverse causality. A firm that undertakes organizational change to achieve sustainability
may increase the issuance of sustainable debt, rather than issuing sustainable debt which
triggers the firm to introduce organizational change. We confirm the endogeneity problem
by regressing sustainable debt on organizational change; we find that the latter increases the
amount of sustainable debt (scaled) by 4.1%.
To mitigate endogeneity concerns, we use identification through heteroskedasticity (see
Rigobon [2003] and Rigobon and Sack [2003]) and generate causal generalized method of
moments (GMM) estimates. The literature on identification through heteroskedasticity sug-
gests that a system of simultaneous equations can be resolved due to a change in variance
of one variable with respect to another, even if there are more unknowns than knowns. The
simplest intuition can be gained by considering a special case: splitting the sample into two
regimes and assuming that in the second regime, sustainable governance is more volatile than
in the first, while the variance in sustainable debt issuances remains constant across the two
regimes. This increase in the variance of sustainable governance implies that the cloud of
realizations enlarges through the sustainable debt schedule. The residuals are distributed
over an ellipse, and the shift in the variance implies a tilting toward the sustainable debt
curve. From the instrumental variables perspective, this is equivalent to having a proba-
bilistic instrument. In sum, if both variances shift by the same amount, the system is not
identified. On the other hand, the system can be identified by the difference in relative
3
variance between the two regimes for sustainable debt issuances and sustainable governance.
For a robust exogenous analysis of regime shifts and parameter stability, we leverage
the unforeseen emergence of the novel coronavirus and the ensuing economic downturn that
began in February 2020. We divide our dataset into three periods surrounding this event:
2013-2018, 2019-2020, and 2021-2022. From a methodological standpoint, this division acts
as a form of probabilistic instrument; in the first regime, we cannot definitively assert that
there is a shift in the pattern of organizational changes. However, in the second regime, the
dynamics of organizational change are noticeably altered as a result of the shock, allowing us
to more accurately discern the relationship between organizational changes and sustainable
debt issuances. The third regime helps us to test the stability of the structural parameters,
and we show that our results are robust to any combination of regimes and close to an
all-regime model.
Upon generating the causal generalized method of moments (GMM)estimates, we find
that a 1% increase in the amount of sustainable debt issuance increases the probability of
adoption of sustainable governance by 9.2%. These findings are statistically significant at
the 1% level. We confirm these results using the number of sustainable bond issuances as
an alternative proxy for the sustainable debt measure. These results show that OLS under-
estimates the causal effect because simultaneity biases the coefficient toward zero. The true
causal effect is 67% larger than the naive estimate. This implies that studies and policy eval-
uations that used ordinary least square (OLS) to assess the governance impact of green bond
markets under-estimate the real organizational impact by approximately two-thirds. Addi-
tionally, we observe that superior governance tends to attract increased investment, a finding
well-documented in the prior literature. This indicates that, particularly when addressing
the endogenous nature of investment and governance, investment also drives governance
improvements, not just the other way around. Our methodology causally demonstrates this.
Our results also show that investment drives governance more strongly than governance
drives investment (9.2% versus 4.2%) which suggests that the traditional view in corporate
finance, that governance reforms are needed to attract investment, is incomplete for sustain-
able markets. These results provide evidence that organizational reform follows capital flows
This reversal of the conventional governance-investment sequence has implications for how
regulators should sequence policy interventions: mandating sustainable debt instruments
may be more effective at inducing governance reform than mandating governance structures
to attract sustainable capital.
Although our GMM estimates are comparable to Iliev and Roth [2023] which find that
4
director exposure to foreign ESG regulation increases the probability of ESG committee
formation by approximately 8–12 percentage points. Our methodology for identification
dominates the quasi-natural experiment used in Iliev and Roth [2023] because latter suf-
fers from verification issue of exclusion restriction, instrument intensity, and the deviation
of Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE) from Average Treatment Effect (ATE). The
identification through heteroskedasticity is free from such issues.4
Beyond addressing endogeneity concerns, we expand our analysis through a series of
additional tests. Aswani and Rajgopal [2025] suggests that the market shows a preference
for sustainable bonds issued by firms in the financial sector, as evidenced by a positive
shareholder reaction and the presence of a greenium in the secondary market. Therefore,
we specifically examine the impact within financial and high-pollution sectors. Our findings
indicate a more pronounced effect among financial sector firms compared to those in polluting
sectors.
Considering that shareholder rights differ across jurisdictions (see Porta et al. [1998]),
we further dissect our results based on the legal framework of the firms’ home countries,
distinguishing between common law and civil law systems. Our analysis demonstrates that
our findings hold particularly strongly in civil law countries, which typically feature weaker
corporate governance systems compared to their common law counterparts. We show that, in
such countries, investment inspires governance more strongly than in common law countries,
where investors are protected by law.
In the second part of the paper, we evaluate whether a firm’s adoption of sustainable
governance effectively streamlines sustainable investment and, more importantly, mitigates
negative externalities. We contend that sustainable governance serves as a complementary
monitoring tool alongside shareholder oversight of a firm’s sustainability efforts. Further-
more, we assert that for firms engaged in sustainable investing, implementing sustainable
governance is unlikely to be merely a marketing strategy, due to the associated costs and the
existing monitoring conducted by pro-social shareholders. With this perspective in mind,
we assess the impact of sustainable governance on the firm’s future sustainable performance.
Our results indicate that sustainable governance can enhance a firm’s environmental per-
formance by 16% to 18%. These results are 2.5–4 times larger than Dyck et al. [2023]’s
estimates which find that adoption of majority voting for directors increases future environ-
mental performance scores by approximately 4–7 percentage points (depending on specifica-
tion). However, in our results, this improvement in environmental performance is limited to

non-financial firms. When we analyzed the environmental performance of sustainable loan
borrowers who borrowed the amount from financial firms that issued sustainable debt and
made changes in sustainable governance, we did not find significant improvement. In con-

governance are insignificant, implying that firms with better environmental performance have
a lower chance of adopting sustainable governance. These results are intuitive, as firms with
better environmental performance would not adopt sustainable governance if the benefits
are marginal compared to the cost of adoption.
Our research draws parallels with Starmans et al. [2026] and Wintoki et al. [2012]. A
recent theory paper by Starmans et al. [2026] predicts that sustainable investing can weaken
the governance role of financial markets by reducing the sensitivity of stock prices to infor-

authors hypothesize that pro-social investors would exit firms with weak environmental and
social (E & S) performance even if the firms have exceptional financial performance. It
would lead to a decline in informed trading, reduce price informativeness, and lower a firm’s
financial performance. In our work, we show that sustainable investment motivates firms to
adopt sustainable governance practices, thereby improving their sustainable performance.
Wintoki et al. [2012] revisits the relationship between board structure and firm perfor-
mance using the Generalized Method of Moments (GMM) estimator, concluding that there is
no causal link between board structure and contemporaneous firm performance. This study
importantly highlights the biases inherent in traditional estimators that neglect the dynamic
interplay between current governance structures and historical firm performance. In a vein
similar to Wintoki et al. [2012], our application of the GMM model, particularly identified
by heteroskedasticity, demonstrates that changes in the sustainable governance structure
improve sustainable performance. We also show that investment significantly encourages
firms to augment governance practices, rather than the reverse. Our findings corroborate
the notion that standard panel regressions, even when adjusted with fixed effects, tend to
bias the magnitude of effects owing to simultaneity concerns. This reinforcement of the dy-
namics between investment, governance, and performance adds nuance to the discourse on
corporate governance effectiveness.

ing and to the literature on the association between investment and corporate governance.
Although the theoretical foundation of signaling was established by Spence (1973), it was
introduced to finance by Ross (1977). Traditional work on signaling in finance is dominated
6
by dividends, debt ratios, capital expenditure, institutional ownership, ownership concen-
tration, and equity issuances as signals that firms use to mitigate information asymmetry.
Firms differentiate themselves from others in the market by bearing the cost of these signals,
which is shown as separation equilibria in the literature.5 Nevertheless, there is hardly any
evidence in the literature about changes in corporate governance structure, ESG disclosure,
and sustainability reporting as corporate signals.
In this paper, we argue that the adoption of sustainable governance signals to sustain-
able investors the firm’s commitment. Investing in observable signals, such as hiring a chief
sustainability officer (CSO) or forming a CSR/ESG committee, assures investors about the
firm’s sustainability prospects. Firms adopt these governance changes because sustainable
investment (such as green bonds) requires reporting compliance, which includes the devel-
opment of impact reports, use-of-proceeds accounts, and third-party certifications required
under the Green Bond Principles. These governance changes help achieve compliance lev-
els and attain targeted environmental performance. Therefore, incurring the cost of these
governance changes serves as an observable signal to investors that firms are serious about
implementing sustainable projects.

et al. [2000], Gugler et al. [2004]) or on understanding the role of debt holders or institu-

[2022]). In the most of these papers, rather than determining these relationships jointly,
they were treated as orthogonal to each other. As corporate governance and firm value are
endogenous, so is corporate governance and investment, since firm value is an important
determinant of the latter. Our paper jointly estimates these relationships and finds that the
impact of investment on governance is stronger than the role of governance in attracting
investment.
Our work also contributes to the emerging literature on sustainable governance. Iliev

overall sustainability performance but also increase the likelihood of forming a sustainability

firms. Their research, which examines the adoption of majority voting for directors and the

6.B. Does Sustainable Governance Improve Sustainable Performance?
In the first section, we demonstrate that sustainable debt encourages firms to adopt sus-
tainable governance practices. Since investment and governance decisions are endogenous,
we use Rigobon (2003) methodology to provide causal evidence that the adoption of sustain-
able governance is driven by sustainable investment. It is still essential to examine whether a
firm’s adoption of sustainable governance effectively streamlines sustainable investment and
mitigates negative externalities.
We acknowledge that we are not the first to have investigated this question. Dyck et al.
[2023] analyze a global sample of 3,293 firms, demonstrating that quasi-exogenous shocks in
corporate governance—such as the adoption of majority voting for directors and the intro-

Heath et al. [2023] show that although SRI funds choose portfolio firms based on higher ‘E’
and ‘S’ performances, these funds are inefficient in improving these performances further.
Thus, the real impact of SRI funds is inconsistent with their claimed impact. A recent
theory paper by Starmans et al. [2026] predicts that sustainable investing can weaken the
governance role of financial markets by reducing the sensitivity of stock prices to information
about firm fundamentals, particularly when firm externalities are significant. The authors
hypothesize that pro-social investors would exit firms with weak environmental and social
(E & S) performance even if the firms have exceptional financial performance. It would lead
to a decline in informed trading and would reduce price informativeness and firm’s financial
performance. To compensate, the shareholders must incentivize the manager to improve the
firm’s performance. As incentives are costly, shareholders may choose to reduce these pro-
visions optimally. This would lead to lower managerial effort and would diminish financial
performance.

nance, prompted by sustainable investing, drives sustainable performance. We contend that
sustainable governance serves as a complementary monitoring tool alongside shareholder

in sustainable investing, implementing sustainable governance is unlikely to be merely a

7. CONCLUSION
This paper examines the dynamics through which sustainable investment motivates firms
to adopt governance structures oriented toward sustainability. Using a global sample of
24
10,970 firms merged with 3,944 sustainable debt issuances, we find that a 1% increase in
sustainable debt issuances raises the likelihood of adopting sustainable governance practices
by 3.7%.
As prior literature has demonstrated that superior corporate governance attracts invest-
ment, we retest this theory and find that improving sustainable governance practices—either
by hiring a chief sustainability officer or establishing an ESG/CSR committee—increases the
amount of sustainable debt issuance by 1%. However, these estimates are biased due to the
simultaneity issue.
To address the simultaneity issue, we employ a Generalized Method of Moments (GMM)
model utilizing a probabilistic instrument based on heteroskedasticity. Our findings reveal
that a 1% increase in sustainable debt (as a proportion of total debt) enhances sustainable
governance by 9.2%. These results remain robust whether we measure sustainable debt
by the number of issuances or the amount issued (scaled by total debt), or when using
alternative ESG databases. These findings suggest that OLS regression, even with fixed
effects, underestimates the coefficients. This core relationship underscores the catalytic role
of financial investment in driving corporate governance reforms.
Our analysis builds upon and diverges from existing literature, such as the study by
Wintoki et al. [2012], which explores the dynamic relationship between board structure
and firm performance but finds no causal linkage. In contrast, our results indicate that
sustainable investment actively promotes better governance, countering the notion of a non-
causal relationship and highlighting the importance of examining these variables within the
context of sustainability.
To enhance the robustness of our findings, we conduct sub-sample analyses based on legal
framework (comparing common law and civil law countries) and sector (contrasting financial
with pollution-intensive industries). While these analyses serve to deepen our understanding,
they reveal that the fundamental relationship between investment and governance remains
significant across different legal and sectoral contexts, albeit with varying magnitudes.
In the second part of the paper, we evaluate whether a firm’s adoption of sustainable
governance effectively streamlines sustainable investment and, more importantly, mitigates
negative externalities, or whether it merely serves as an advertising gimmick supporting
greenwashing claims. We argue that sustainable governance serves as a complementary
monitoring tool alongside shareholder oversight of a firm’s sustainability efforts. Further-
more, we contend that for firms engaged in sustainable investing, implementing sustainable
governance is unlikely to be merely a marketing strategy, given the associated costs and the
25
existing monitoring conducted by pro-social shareholders. With this perspective in mind,
we assess the impact of sustainable governance on the firm’s future sustainable performance.
Our results indicate that sustainable investing can enhance a firm’s environmental perfor-
mance through improvements in sustainable governance.
The findings of this paper reaffirm the significant impact of sustainable debt on gov-
ernance improvements across diverse global settings. However, we acknowledge that the
transformative power of such investments can be influenced by the legal environment and
the operational sector of the firm. Notably, while the core relationship is universal, the ex-
tent of governance enhancement is more pronounced in civil law countries, potentially due
to weaker pre-existing shareholder protections compared to their common law counterparts.
Furthermore, the impact of sustainable debt on governance is more discernible within the
financial sector, likely reflecting the sector’s pivotal role in the transition toward sustainabil-
ity.
Extending our analysis to understand the role of sustainable governance, we find that
sustainable investing can enhance a firm’s environmental performance by improving its sus-
tainable governance. The causal GMM estimates suggest that sustainable governance im-
proves the environmental performance of a firm by 16% to 18%. These results hold only for
non-financial firms; for financial firms, to improve sustainable performance, there is an ad-
ditional requirement for due-diligence beyond adopting sustainable governance. We believe
that these findings contribute to the ongoing debate on relation between sustainable invest-
ment and corporate governance, providing valuable insights for academicians, policymakers,
investors, and corporations striving toward a sustainable future.

Abstract
Background
Loss to follow-up (LTFU) during tuberculosis treatment is a major programmatic gap, but how much excess mortality it causes has been difficult to estimate, because individuals who disengage differ from those who do not, and they must survive long enough to be recorded as having disengaged. Quantifying this excess and identifying which populations are at greatest risk are critical to informing program design and resource allocation.
Methods and findings
We followed 171,048 people aged 15 years or older starting a first course of tuberculosis treatment in São Paulo State, Brazil, between 2013 and 2023, linking surveillance and mortality registries; 20,830 (12.2%) were LTFU, defined as interruption of treatment for at least 30 consecutive days. Among those LTFU, 65% had received directly observed therapy (DOT). Using a clone-censor-weight target trial emulation, we contrasted two strategies over 60 months from the first day of treatment: disengagement at any point during the first 6 months and remaining in care throughout. Analyses were adjusted for age, sex, race, education, HIV status, diabetes, alcohol use, drug use, incarceration, homelessness, hospitalization at diagnosis, clinical form of tuberculosis, DOT, and municipality. A rolling landmark analysis addressed the timing of disengagement and cause-specific mortality excess. LTFU increased standardized 5-year mortality by 2.49 percentage points (95% CI [1.94, 3.17]). In a rolling landmark analysis, tuberculosis accounted for 61% of the 5-year excess mortality. Relative effects were largest in younger, stably housed individuals, whose baseline mortality was low; the largest absolute excess fell on people living with HIV (5.16 percentage points, 95% CI [3.76, 6.60]). The excess was similar for disengagement at any point in the first 4 months of treatment and attenuated thereafter. Limitations include the absence from the registry of severity markers such as radiographic extent and bacillary load, so residual confounding cannot be excluded.
Conclusions
Despite high DOT coverage, disengagement during the first 6 months of tuberculosis treatment was common and increased 5-year mortality under the stated identification assumptions, with the excess concentrated in deaths attributed to tuberculosis. Interventions that provide support throughout treatment should be tested for their effectiveness in sustaining engagement and reducing mortality.
Author summary
Why was this study done?
- People who interrupt tuberculosis treatment have a higher risk of death, but it remains unclear how much of this risk is attributable to treatment interruption itself.
- Estimating this impact is challenging because people who interrupt treatment differ from those who remain in care, and the way these groups are compared can lead to misleading results.
- Understanding how treatment interruption affects deaths from tuberculosis and other causes, including years after treatment begins, is important for improving tuberculosis care.
What did the researchers do and find?
- We studied 171,048 people starting tuberculosis treatment in São Paulo State, Brazil, between 2013 and 2023, using health records to examine mortality over 5 years.
- We estimated that interrupting treatment increased the 5-year risk of death by ~25 additional deaths per 1,000 people, with tuberculosis itself the leading cause of these additional deaths.
- The increase in mortality was similar when treatment was interrupted during any of the first 4 months after starting treatment, and people living with HIV experienced the largest absolute increase in risk.
What do these findings mean?
- Interrupting tuberculosis treatment may contribute to deaths occurring years after treatment begins, making sustained engagement in care important for long-term survival.
- Although most people who interrupted treatment had received directly observed therapy, our findings suggest that tuberculosis programs need approaches that go beyond observing medication intake to help patients complete treatment.
- Because the study used routinely collected health records, we could not fully account for differences in disease severity or changes in patients’ health during treatment, and some patients were excluded because of incomplete records or transfers.
